item.title: Wall Street bosses look past India's pain points to ramp up investment bets
item.description: Wall Street bosses are still looking at the economy's long-term prospects. Many are betting on a series of measures taken by the Modi administration to jumpstart a vast digital payments ecosystem ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Preeti Singh, Ranjani Raghavan, Saikat Das and Siddhi Nayak Across India’s small towns and bustling cities, retail investors have been snapping up shares of newly listed companies. It’s a boom that Blackstone Inc.’s President Jon Gray celebrates thousands of miles away in his Park Avenue office.  “For us, outside of the United States, India is the most liquid market — the easiest place to get an IPO done in the world this year,’’ Gray said in an interview. India already saw one of its biggest ever initial public offerings in recent weeks and a listing with a market value of more than $100 billion is possible from billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s empire, making the country one of the world’s busiest IPO markets.  Gray and other financial heavyweights acknowledge challenges like rising inflation and the falling rupee. Yet, between its private equity and real estate businesses, Blackstone has listed a string of companies over the past decade in India and revenue growth has been high, Gray said. The firm expects assets under management in the South Asian country to double to $100 billion in the coming years. That’s a sign of the growing sophistication of the financial markets within this $4 trillion economy as it opens up further to foreign money. It’s also a dramatic turnaround from just a few years ago when private equity investors had limited options to exit investments in India, let alone at substantial profits. Now private equity, private credit and sovereign wealth funds are committing ever deeper pools of capital, while market makers like Citadel Securities LLC and hedge funds like Millennium Management LLC have built a presence there. Other parts of the financial industry are also changing swiftly.  India’s markets remain a fraction of China’s by size. High corporate taxes and the rupee’s decline leave foreign firms smaller profits to repatriate into dollars. On the political front, a youth protest movement is creating new pressures for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government.  Wall Street bosses are still looking at the economy’s long-term prospects. Many are betting on a series of measures taken by the Modi administration to jumpstart a vast digital payments ecosystem. Millions of Indians are now putting their savings into financial markets for the first time. As new developments reshape Indian finance, here are some of the biggest changes and challenges emerging: Banking Boom In recent months, a string of Wall Street bosses have landed in India to court businesses and the government. Citigroup Inc.’s Jane Fraser had a meeting with Modi. JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Jamie Dimon met the country’s finance minister. Both firms are working on the IPO of Ambani’s digital services giant Jio Platforms. That company is expected to go public later this year at a valuation that could make it India’s largest ever, Bloomberg News has reported.   Banks have been bolstering teams in investment banking and capital markets. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. has injected at least $500 million into its India banking franchise in recent years, Bloomberg News has reported. It’s also one of the banks on the Jio IPO.  “Rapid financialization of household savings is creating a durable pool of domestic capital to support private-sector investment,” said Sonjoy Chatterjee, chairman and chief executive officer of Goldman Sachs India.  The average fee paid to bankers in India has risen to 1.86% of an IPO’s value, according to capital-markets data provider LSEG. That’s higher than roughly 1.5% in Hong Kong. The firms are all vying for a larger slice of the pie in what’s become one of the world’s most competitive investment banking markets. The Wall Street banks are competing against each other as well as Japanese ones and local firms like Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. and Axis Bank Ltd., who command deep client relationships and pricing power.  Meanwhile, global banks are seeing other opportunities. Citi's India CEO K. Balasubramanian said in an interview that the bank sees added opportunities to do business with local and foreign corporations as India enters into more trade deals with countries including the UK. The India arm of Japan's Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. plans to expand its rupee-bond business as companies diversify funding, according to a spokesperson. It has managed about 57 billion rupees ($600 million) of local bonds since the inception of its business in September 2025 and aims to significantly enhance its share over the next two to three years. The firm is also expanding in India’s IPO market. Private Equity Money Until the 1990s, India was almost completely closed to foreign capital, and few private equity funds were involved in major deals. As the economy has opened up, PE firms have invested tens of billions of dollars and deal sizes have been increasing.   Brookfield Asset Management Ltd.’s CEO Connor Teskey says that over the next five years the firm’s investment in India will be more than $100 billion from about $30 billion in 2025. It’s a bet on “India’s immense scale, strong economic growth, respect for capital and growing demand for infrastructure,” he said.  Firms like Brookfield and Blackstone are also betting on the country’s real estate markets. Office space has seen a boom as local and foreign companies scramble for room in swanky new towers in cities like Mumbai and New Delhi.  “The one challenge obviously has been higher inflation rates and currency depreciation,” Gray said. Despite that Blackstone has had very good success in areas like its logistics portfolio because “there’s so much underlying demand that you can make up for the fact that the currency’s been going down,” he said.  Global Capability Centers The basic back-office centers that began in the 1990s have evolved into mission-critical cogs of global finance. India had more than 1,800 Global Capability Centers in 2025 and that is projected to exceed 2,400 by 2030, according to a Dun & Bradstreet report.  While low-end jobs have been shifting to places like the Philippines, the sprawling Indian campuses house armies of quants, risk analysts, investment and tech staff.  GCCs are estimated to have generated around $100 billion in revenue last fiscal year. They have grown so much that some Wall Street giants have more employees in India than anywhere else outside the US. JPMorgan alone has around 60,000 people working at its India GCCs.  Minting Millionaires Only a small percentage of people in this nation of nearly 1.5 billion people are presently invested in markets, despite recent improvements. Indians save $500 billion annually in financial assets and almost 50% of that is still in cash and deposits, according to analysts at Macquarie. More of their money may now flow overseas. In recent weeks, India’s market regulator has said it will allow a $463 billion segment of its portfolio management industry catering to wealthy individuals to invest in overseas securities and short equity options.  India’s population of ultra-high-net-worth individuals is forecast to rise from about 19,000 in 2026 to roughly 25,000 by 2031, underscoring its growing role in the global wealth landscape, according to a Knight Frank report. That’s enabled established international private banks like Standard Chartered Plc and HSBC Holdings Plc to build sizeable franchises. Still, the wealth boom has brought a new set of problems for Modi. As one section of Indian society has grown richer, inequities have deepened and sparked social upheaval. Youth discontent burst into public view this year through the Cockroach Janta Party, a movement that began as satire after a Supreme Court judge compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches. As young people took to the streets  this weekend, the authorities imposed unprecedented restrictions in New Delhi, deploying thousands of police and asking telecom operators to suspend internet services near protest areas.  Mixed Markets While longer term investments have poured in, India’s markets have taken a hit this year as the oil importing country’s currency has slumped and inflation has risen with higher crude prices. Foreign portfolio institutions have pulled out about $30 billion from domestic stocks so far this year in pursuit of artificial intelligence opportunities elsewhere.   While India is among the worst-performing equity markets in 2026, its capital markets have deepened and matured rapidly since the pandemic, underpinned partly by sticky domestic flows, the IPO boom and wide-ranging investment opportunities.  Growing liquidity and institutional participation continue to make the country an important destination in global portfolios. High frequency trading desks run by firms like Optiver Holding BV are going head-to-head with newly minted Indian trading joints and are fueling a fight for top talent. At some high frequency firms, interns have begun to command $31,000 in monthly pay in India.  Regulatory Challenges New dilemmas are emerging for India’s regulators as its markets become more liquid. Indian retail traders lost more than $9 billion trading equity futures and options in the year ended March.  That’s pushed India’s regulators to clamp down on a boom in the options and futures market, one of the most lucrative areas for foreign trading desks.  The regulator recently accused a small Mauritius-based JPMorgan unit of executing manipulative stock trades in India. The offshore unit’s trading ban has since been lifted. Last year, in one of its most dramatic actions on a foreign firm, SEBI accused Jane Street of market manipulation, an allegation that the US financial giant has denied. The firm has pressed ahead with its case in a high-profile appeal against India’s securities regulator.  GIFT City Rises A new free market oasis called GIFT City is seeing a boom. Gujarat International Finance Tec-City is part of Modi’s push to develop a hub in India that can compete with major international cities. Foreign banks are seeing assets surge in this alternative low-tax center on India’s west coast. There, they are helping set up treasury operations for corporations, offering financing for international businesses and helping foreign clients trade. HSBC has built a $23 billion balance sheet in GIFT city in under six years, according to people familiar with the matter. Citi’s assets there are likely to reach $3 billion by the end of 2026 from about $350 million last December, its India CEO K. Balasubramanian said. The hub is “central to the internationalization of India’s economy and to building a global financial hub onshore,” he said. “That makes it a big focus for Citi.”

item.title: Logistics sector must prepare workforce for tech shift: Skill council
item.description: The Logistics Sector Skill Council (LSC) in Chennai hosted PRISM 2026 - Powering Recognition: India's Skill Movement, an industry connect meet ...
item.dc:creator: Shine Jacob
item.content:encoded: India's logistics sector is undergoing a transformation driven by technology, automation, and digitisation, and the industry should prepare its workforce to adapt to these changes, a top executive of the Logistics Sector Skill Council has said. The Logistics Sector Skill Council (LSC) in Chennai hosted PRISM 2026 – Powering Recognition: India’s Skill Movement, an industry connect meet. It brought together senior government officials, industry leaders, representatives of Sector Skill Councils, education and training institutions, and key stakeholders from across India’s skilling ecosystem. It deliberated on the future of workforce development in the logistics sector. Cyrus Guzder, chairman, Logistics Sector Skill Council, said, “India’s logistics sector is undergoing a fundamental transformation, driven by technology, automation, digitalisation and growing global integration. Our focus must move beyond simply training people to building a workforce that is employable, adaptable and capable of meeting global standards. PRISM provides a platform for stakeholders to come together, understand emerging requirements and translate those insights into meaningful action.” Centred on the theme “India’s Logistics Workforce for Global Competitiveness,” PRISM 2026 focused on evolving industry skill requirements and the need to build a future-ready workforce capable of adapting to technological advancements, emerging career opportunities and the growing integration of India’s logistics sector with global supply chains. PRISM 2026 reinforced the need for a coordinated approach to workforce development, with industry providing demand insights and workplace exposure, government enabling an appropriate policy environment, and the skilling ecosystem translating emerging requirements into relevant qualifications, training programmes and assessment frameworks. The discussions underscored the growing significance of logistics in India’s economic ambitions and highlighted the importance of strengthening collaboration between government, industry and the skilling ecosystem to ensure workforce development keeps pace with the sector’s rapid transformation. S Padmanabhan, board director, LSC and representative of the logistics industry, said, “The logistics industry needs the right talent, with the right skills, at the right time. Industry must be a partner in skilling and not merely a consumer of skilled talent. We need to work closely with LSC, government and training institutions to ensure that training is connected to real workplace requirements and that young people see logistics as a sector offering long-term and rewarding careers.” PRISM 2026 featured discussions on the changing dynamics of the logistics industry and the skills required to prepare its workforce for the future. The session titled “Building a Future-Ready Logistics Workforce – Skill Demand and Sector Transformation” examined evolving industry requirements and the need to align training and workforce development with emerging business and operational priorities. The subsequent session, “Workforce 4.0,” explored the impact of artificial intelligence, automation, global mobility and emerging careers on the logistics talent landscape. The discussions emphasised the importance of continuous upskilling and reskilling to ensure that India’s workforce remains relevant and competitive as technology reshapes job roles, processes and operating models. Another key discussion, “The SSC Toolkit,” examined how Sector Skill Councils can support industry through government schemes, policy incentives and effective implementation mechanisms. The session highlighted opportunities to strengthen collaboration among industry, government and training institutions to address skill gaps and improve the relevance and effectiveness of skilling initiatives. A key highlight of the discussions was India’s achievement at WorldSkills Shanghai 2026, where the country won a silver medal in logistics and freight forwarding. The accomplishment demonstrated the potential of Indian logistics talent to compete at international standards and reinforced the importance of creating more opportunities for young professionals to develop advanced skills and pursue global careers. The achievement also highlighted the need for stronger industry participation in skills development through workplace exposure, apprenticeships, practical training and industry-aligned curricula. Closer engagement between employers and training institutions will be critical to ensuring that young professionals acquire the competencies required to succeed in a rapidly evolving global logistics environment. The event culminated in the PRISM Awards – “Powering Recognition: India’s Skill Movement,” recognising contributions and achievements that support the growth and development of India’s skilling ecosystem. The awards highlighted the importance of recognising not only individual excellence but also the contributions of institutions, industry partners and other stakeholders working to strengthen employability, encourage innovation and advance workforce development. The discussions also emphasised the importance of establishing clear career pathways, encouraging lifelong learning and ensuring that India’s logistics workforce is equipped to support the country’s expanding domestic and international logistics requirements. Through PRISM, the Logistics Sector Skill Council reaffirmed its commitment to working closely with government, industry, academia, training partners and other stakeholders to build an industry-led, future-focused and globally competitive logistics workforce. As India strengthens its position in global supply chains and advances its economic ambitions, collaborative and industry-aligned skilling will remain central to developing the talent required to power the next phase of growth in the logistics sector.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / News / TCS to hire 80% of workforce with digital, AI skills; expects margin gains

TCS to hire 80% of workforce with digital, AI skills; expects margin gains TCS said 80% of its new hires will have digital and AI skills, with AI-led work contributing 10% of revenue in Q2

With the share of AI-led work in overall revenue growing to 10 per cent in the recently concluded September quarter, the country's largest IT services company said a growth in the share of AI revenues will help it expand its profit margins (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 12:30 PM IST

Listen to This Article

As much as 80 per cent of TCS' new hires will be talent with digital and Artificial Intelligence (AI) skills going forward, a top company official has said. With the share of AI-led work in overall revenue growing to 10 per cent in the recently concluded September quarter, the country's largest IT services company said a growth in the share of AI revenues will help it expand its profit margins, which remain below its aspirational levels. "Of the 4,500 that we have added in Q2, I would say safely 25 to 30 per cent are pure AI and total about 80 per cent is new age," the company's chief operating officer Arathi Subramanian told PTI here.

When asked if the same proportion will continue going ahead as well, she replied in the affirmative and added that the desired talent is available in the market. When asked if it is advantage for freshers over the mid-career professionals in this sort environment, where their AI-nativity and relatively lower costs would be of help to the former, she said that it is advantage for people willing to "unlearn and learn". "If a mid-level engineer is willing to learn, it gives a huge advantage because he or she understands what is the technology landscape, what is the domain," the company's chief executive and managing director K Krithivasan added, pointing out that a junior engineer may not be able to understand the same.

The company will continue investing in "niche talent" going forward as well, Krithivasan said, adding that mergers and acquisitions and partnerships will be other areas of investments. Krithivasan said the trend of growth in AI revenues will also help from a profitability perspective. "As these (AI) deals increase in volume, you would see that there will be margin (benefit)," he said. Subramanian said customers are signing up for an AI deal in a small vertical, and expanding then asking for an expansion of the same work in other areas as well once the efficacy of the spending gets established. To a question on what is the proportion of AI in new deal signings and how much of the USD 9.6 billion in total contract value of Q2 is AI, Krithivasan said the company is very conservative while classifying a deal as a an AI one, but added that there is some aspect of AI in virtually all the work that it is doing at present.

When asked if two recent deal wins on Porsche and Best Buy, where a contract is accompanied with absorbing the clients' staff into TCS, portends to challenges in the market, Krithivasan replied in the negative. "These two are opportunities where our customers come to us and we have discussions on how we help them transform themselves and make them AI first," he said.

item.description: TCS chief executive and managing director K Krithivasan said companies are 'deeply ingrained' in the US' technology ecosystem and provide an important service ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / Don't see US acting against tech companies based on their domicile: TCS

Don't see US acting against tech companies based on their domicile: TCS TCS chief executive and managing director K Krithivasan said companies are 'deeply ingrained' in the US' technology ecosystem and provide an important service

TCS, which has been sending staff to the US when clients demand so, applied for only 10 or so green cards last year (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 11:35 AM IST

Listen to This Article

India's largest IT services company TCS feels that the US is unlikely to target tech companies based on their domicile and actions like last week's decision to suspend a green card application programme are driven by local sensitivities around jobs. TCS chief executive and managing director K Krithivasan said companies are "deeply ingrained" in the US' technology ecosystem and provide an important service. "I do not think the governments will really look at it from a domicile perspective. I think what the governments have been looking at is from an employment perspective," Krithivasan told PTI in an interview at the company's corporate headquarters here.   Sensitivities around local job creation may be leading the governments to take actions like the one against the eight companies including TCS, Krithivasan said, stressing that the last week's decision has no material impact for the largest Indian IT services company. TCS, which has been sending staff to the US when clients demand so, applied for only 10 or so green cards last year, he said, adding that the overall H1-B visa applications were less than 300. Also Read

No impact of Tata Sons board tussle on TCS: COO Aarthi Subramanian premium

Infosys sees no material impact from US suspension of PERM applications

TCS withholds quarterly bonuses for senior staff after missing targets

Many of the H1-B applications consisted of people already in the US, he said, making it clear that there was no fresh employee sent to the country from India. When quizzed about the mid-term polls in November and how the company looks at it, Krithivasan said TCS has a long-term strategy in the US, its biggest market by revenues, and the election outcome will not lead to any change in it. As part of the efforts to be involved in every geography that it operates in, the TCS focus is on local hires, he said, adding that over half of the over 30,000 people it employs in the US are locals. To a question on whether the promise to add another 15,000 people in the US over the next five years spelt out earlier involves adding only US citizens, its chief operating officer Arathi Subramanian said the company hires diverse talent who fulfil the skill requirements but made it clear that nationality of a person is not important. "We have this deep experience of integrating into the geography and benefit from the diversity," she said, conceding that there may be people of Indian origin, including those born in the US or who have migrated earlier. After the US suspended eight tech firms, including prominent Indian ones, from a key green card programme, industry body Nasscom said immigration and skilled talent mobility are "two distinct issues" that should not be viewed through the same lens. The latest action comes amid mounting challenges for Indian IT companies in the US, including tighter scrutiny of work visas and higher costs for H-1B applicants. The latest development in the US -- the biggest market for the USD 300-billion Indian IT industry -- adds to uncertainty for tech outsourcers that rely on the cross-border movement of skilled professionals.
